Language review 4 › Sense verbs | أفعال.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)

questions.q: Which group of words names the five senses?
options: sight, hearing, taste, touch and smell
look, sound, taste, feel and smell
sight, listening, flavour, touch and nose
seeing, hearing, eating, feeling and smelling
questions.topic: the five senses
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: The lesson names the five senses as sight, hearing, taste, touch and smell.

questions.q: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: *Her new dress looks ____.*
options: beautiful
beautifully
beauty
beautify
questions.topic: adjective after the sense verb look
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: After the sense verb *look* we use an adjective (*beautiful*), not an adverb.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct sense verb: *I can't see the actors, but their voices ____ very clear.*
options: look
sound
taste
smell
questions.topic: sound for the sense of hearing
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *sound* goes with the sense of hearing, so we say the voices sound clear.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the verb: *The verbs that ____ our five senses are look, sound, taste, feel and smell.*
options: expresses
expressed
express
expressing
questions.topic: subject–verb agreement: verbs that express
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: The subject *verbs* is plural, so the verb must be *express*, not *expresses*.

questions.q: Why is *It smells great!* correct, but *It smells greatly!* wrong?
options: Because sense verbs are followed by an adjective, not an adverb.
Because *greatly* is only used with the verb *feel*.
Because *smell* is a noun and cannot take an adverb.
Because the sentence needs *does* before the verb.
questions.topic: why sense verbs take adjectives, not adverbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: Sense verbs are usually followed by an adjective, so *It smells great* is correct.

questions.q: What is the difference between these two sentences? *The soup smells nice.* / *The soup tastes nice.*
options: The first describes a taste, the second describes a smell.
The first describes a smell, the second describes a taste.
Both sentences describe what we see.
The first describes a sound, the second describes a touch.
questions.topic: smell vs taste
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *smell* is used for the nose and *taste* for the tongue.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *She feels badly today.*
options: Change *feels* to *is feel*.
Change *She* to *Her*.
Change *badly* to *bad*.
Change *today* to *today's*.
questions.topic: adjective after feel
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *feel* is followed by the adjective *bad*, not the adverb *badly*.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: The music sounds too loudly.
The music sound too loud.
The music too loud sounds.
The music sounds too loud.
questions.topic: adjective and -s agreement with sound
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *sounds* agrees with *the music*, and an adjective (*loud*) follows the sense verb.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence correctly: *These oranges taste sweetly and smell freshly.*
options: These oranges taste sweetly and smell fresh.
These oranges taste sweet and smell fresh.
These oranges tastes sweet and smells fresh.
These oranges taste sweet and smell freshly.
questions.topic: two adjectives after two sense verbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: Two adjectives are needed here, so *sweetly* becomes *sweet* and *freshly* becomes *fresh*.

questions.q: Make a question for the underlined word: *The soup smells __delicious__.*
options: How does the soup smell?
How the soup smells?
How does the soup smells?
What does the soup smell?
questions.topic: question form with does and a sense verb
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: A present simple question needs *does* + subject + base verb: *How does the soup smell?*

questions.q: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: *The soup tastes ____.*
options: good
well
nicely
greatly
questions.topic: Adjective after sense verbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: A sense verb here describes a state, like the verb *be*, so an adjective (good) follows it, not an adverb.

questions.q: Complete with the correct word: *The new machine sounds ____ a jet engine.*
options: like
as
so
such
questions.topic: like + noun after sense verbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: When a noun follows a sense verb we add *like*: sounds like a jet engine.

questions.q: In which sentence does the word **well** mean 'healthy'?
options: My grandfather is 80, but he still feels well.
She plays the piano well.
The old engine works well now.
He speaks English well.
questions.topic: well as an adjective of health
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *Well* can be an adjective meaning 'in good health', so it is correct after *feel*; in the other sentences it is an adverb of manner.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the verb: *That cake ____ delicious.*
options: smells
smell
smelling
is smell
questions.topic: Subject-verb agreement with sense verbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: The subject *That cake* is singular, so the present simple verb takes -s: smells.

questions.q: Choose the correct words: *The medicine tastes ____ , but it smells ____ honey.*
options: bitter — like
like — bitter
bitterly — like
bitter — as
questions.topic: Adjective vs. like + noun after sense verbs
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: An adjective (bitter) describes the subject, while *like* is added when a noun (honey) comes after the sense verb (smells like honey).

questions.q: Why is *The music sounds loudly* wrong?
options: Because the sense verb here is like *be*, and the adjective describes the subject.
Because the verb *sound* must always be followed by a noun in English.
Because adverbs of manner like *loudly* are used only in the past tense.
Because the word *loudly* is an adjective and not an adverb at all.
questions.topic: Why sense verbs take adjectives
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: After a sense verb the adjective describes the subject, exactly as after the verb *be*; an adverb would describe the verb instead.

questions.q: Which sentence describes an emotion rather than a physical feeling?
options: I feel nervous before every exam.
This blanket feels warm.
The floor feels cold.
My throat feels dry.
questions.topic: feel for emotions vs. physical sensation
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: *Feel* + an adjective of emotion (nervous) tells how someone feels inside, while the other sentences describe physical sensations.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence so that it has the same meaning, using *like*: *These biscuits have the same taste as honey.*
options: These biscuits taste like honey.
These biscuits taste honey.
These biscuits taste as honey.
These biscuits tastes like honey.
questions.topic: Rewriting with like + noun
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: The pattern is sense verb + like + noun, and the plural subject *biscuits* takes *taste*, not *tastes*.

questions.q: Choose the correct words to complete the sentence: *The perfume ____ wonderful, and it ____ roses.*
options: smells — smells like
smells like — smells
smells — smells
smell — smell like
questions.topic: Combining agreement with like + noun
questions.lesson: Sense verbs | أفعال الحواس (look / sound / taste / feel / smell)
questions.why: The subject *The perfume* is singular (smells), and a noun (*roses*) after a sense verb needs *like*.

Language review 2 › Expressing hope for.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل

questions.q: When a speaker says 'I can't wait for the weekend', what do they mean?
options: They are very excited and want the weekend to come soon.
They are worried that the weekend will be too short.
They are sorry that the weekend has finished.
They are not interested in the weekend at all.
questions.topic: meaning of 'I can't wait for'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'I can't wait for' shows strong excitement about something that is still coming.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct word: *I can't wait ____ the summer holiday.*
options: for
to
with
of
questions.topic: 'can't wait' + for + noun
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: Before a noun we use 'for': I can't wait for the summer holiday.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *I can't wait ____ my grandparents in Sana'a next week.*
options: to visit
visiting
visit
for visiting
questions.topic: 'can't wait' + to + infinitive
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: After 'I can't wait' before a verb we use 'to' + base verb: to visit.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *We are looking forward to ____ the new science museum next Sunday.*
options: visiting
visit
visited
to visit
questions.topic: verb + -ing after 'looking forward to'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'To' in 'looking forward to' is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the missing word: *I'm looking forward ____ the school trip next month.*
options: to
for
at
about
questions.topic: the preposition 'to' after 'looking forward'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'Looking forward' is always followed by 'to', never by 'for' or 'at'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *I look forward to ____ from you soon.*
options: hearing
hear
heard
hears
questions.topic: 'look forward to hearing from you' in letters
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: After the preposition 'to' the verb takes -ing: to hearing from you.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: *My sister ____ looking forward to the trip to Aden.*
options: is
are
am
were
questions.topic: subject-verb agreement with 'looking forward to'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'My sister' is singular, so the verb must be 'is'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct pair of words: *I can't wait ____ the Eid holiday, and I can't wait ____ visit my cousins.*
options: for / to
to / for
for / for
to / to
questions.topic: 'for' + noun vs 'to' + verb after 'can't wait'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'Can't wait for' comes before a noun, and 'can't wait to' comes before a verb.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'I can't wait for' and 'I'm looking forward to'?
options: 'I can't wait' is informal and strong; 'looking forward to' fits formal and informal English.
'I can't wait' is formal; 'looking forward to' is only used with close friends.
'I can't wait' talks about the past; 'looking forward to' talks about the future.
They have the same use, and both mean that something has already finished.
questions.topic: difference between 'can't wait' and 'looking forward to'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: The lesson says 'I can't wait' is informal with strong excitement, while 'looking forward to' suits both formal and informal English.

questions.q: Which sentence is informal and shows strong excitement about something that is coming?
options: I can't wait for the school holiday!
I am writing to ask about the school holiday.
I look forward to the school holiday.
I would like to know about the school holiday.
questions.topic: informal use of 'can't wait'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'I can't wait' is the informal phrase, and it carries strong excitement.

questions.q: Which sentence is the best way to finish an email to your teacher?
options: I look forward to hearing from you.
I can't wait to hear from you.
I can't wait for hearing from you.
I'm looking forward to hear from you.
questions.topic: choosing the right closing sentence in an email
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'I look forward to hearing from you' is polite and correct: 'to' is followed by the -ing form.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *I'm looking forward to go to college next year.*
options: I'm looking forward to going to college next year.
I'm looking forward go to college next year.
I'm looking forward to went to college next year.
I'm look forward to going to college next year.
questions.topic: correcting 'looking forward to go'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'To' here is a preposition, so the verb must be 'going', not 'go'.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *They are looking forward the new sports centre.*
options: They are looking forward to the new sports centre.
They are looking forward for the new sports centre.
They are looking forward to visit the new sports centre.
They look forward the new sports centre.
questions.topic: missing 'to' after 'looking forward'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'Looking forward' needs the preposition 'to' before a noun.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *I can't wait the football match on Friday.*
options: I can't wait for the football match on Friday.
I can't wait to the football match on Friday.
I can't wait at the football match on Friday.
I can't wait for seeing the football match on Friday.
questions.topic: missing 'for' after 'can't wait'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: Before a noun, 'can't wait' needs 'for': can't wait for the match.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct pair of words: *I'm looking forward to ____ my aunt in Cairo, and she can't wait ____ me.*
options: visiting / to see
visit / seeing
to visit / to see
visiting / seeing
questions.topic: 'looking forward to' + -ing vs 'can't wait' + to
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: 'Looking forward to' takes the -ing form, while 'can't wait' takes 'to' + base verb.

questions.q: Put the words in the correct order to make a sentence: *forward / are / we / to / the / looking / school / play / .*
options: We are looking forward to the school play.
We are looking forward the school play to.
We looking are forward to the school play.
We are forward looking to the school play.
questions.topic: word order with 'looking forward to'
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: The order is subject + are + looking forward to + noun.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence using 'can't wait': *My family is very excited about the trip to Socotra.*
options: My family can't wait for the trip to Socotra.
My family can't wait to the trip to Socotra.
My family can't wait the trip to Socotra.
My family can't waits for the trip to Socotra.
questions.topic: rewriting with 'can't wait for' + noun
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: The excitement is about a noun (the trip), so we use 'can't wait for'.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence so that it begins with 'She is looking forward to': *She will start her new job in Dubai next month.*
options: She is looking forward to starting her new job in Dubai next month.
She is looking forward to start her new job in Dubai next month.
She is looking forward starting her new job in Dubai next month.
She is look forward to starting her new job in Dubai next month.
questions.topic: rewriting with 'looking forward to' + -ing
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: After the preposition 'to' the verb changes to the -ing form: starting.

questions.q: Combine the two ideas in one sentence using 'can't wait to': *My brother will travel to Egypt next week. He is very excited about it.*
options: My brother can't wait to travel to Egypt next week.
My brother can't wait for to travel to Egypt next week.
My brother can't wait travelling to Egypt next week.
My brother can't waits to travel to Egypt next week.
questions.topic: combining ideas with 'can't wait to' + infinitive
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: When a verb follows, 'can't wait' takes 'to' + base verb: can't wait to travel.

questions.q: Change the sentence so that it is about Huda: *I'm looking forward to meeting my new classmates.*
options: Huda is looking forward to meeting her new classmates.
Huda is looking forward to meeting my new classmates.
Huda is looking forward to meet her new classmates.
Huda looking forward to meeting her new classmates.
questions.topic: changing the subject in a 'looking forward to' sentence
questions.lesson: Expressing hope for the future | التعبير عن الشوق والأمل للمستقبل
questions.why: With the new subject 'Huda' the verb becomes 'is' and the possessive becomes 'her'.

questions.q: Read: *__I'm afraid__ your flight has been delayed.* What does 'I'm afraid' mean in this sentence?
options: I'm frightened of flying
I'm sorry (used to make bad news sound gentler)
I'm not sure about the news
I'm angry about the news
questions.topic: Meaning of 'I'm afraid' in polite requests
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: In the lesson 'I'm afraid' here does not mean 'frightened'; it means 'I'm sorry' and softens unwanted news.

questions.q: Complete with the correct form: *Would you mind ____ me with my homework?*
options: help
to help
helping
helped
questions.topic: Would you mind + verb-ing
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: After 'Would you mind' the verb always takes -ing, so 'helping' is the only correct form.

questions.q: In the lesson, 'you'll have to' is the short form of 'you will have to'. What does this expression mean?
options: You will be able to do something
You would like to do something
You will be obliged to do something
You are allowed to do something
questions.topic: Meaning of 'you'll have to'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'You'll have to' means you are obliged to do something, as in the lesson's note.

questions.q: A: *Would you mind closing the gate?* B: ____ Which reply shows that B agrees to do it?
options: Yes, I do mind.
Not at all.
You're welcome.
I'm afraid so.
questions.topic: Replies to 'Would you mind ...?'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: The question 'Would you mind ...?' is agreed to with 'Not at all.' or 'No, of course not.'

questions.q: *Can you lend me your dictionary?* — Who do you usually say this to?
options: Strangers you have just met
Close friends and family
Older people you do not know
People in an official meeting
questions.topic: Formality: Can vs Could/Would
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'Can you ...?' is the least formal request, used with friends and family; 'Could/Would' are more polite.

questions.q: Read: *Sit down.* Why would the speaker add a word like 'please' or change it into a question form?
options: Because 'please' makes the sentence a question
Because commands are only used in writing
Because a bare command can sound impolite
Because the speaker is angry
questions.topic: Why we soften a bare command
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: A command alone may sound impolite, so we add 'please' or use a question form.

questions.q: Make this command polite with 'Could you ...?': *Open the window.*
options: Could you opening the window?
Could you to open the window?
Could open the window?
Could you open the window?
questions.topic: Turning a command into a 'Could you' request
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'Could you + infinitive' turns a bare command into a polite question.

questions.q: Complete: *____ , but you'll have to show your ticket at the gate.*
options: Not at all
No, of course not
I'm sorry
Would you mind
questions.topic: Softening an obligatory request with 'I'm sorry, but ...'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'I'm sorry, but ...' is used to make an obligatory request sound gentler.

questions.q: Rewrite as a polite request with 'Would you mind': *Bring your notebook to class.*
options: Would you mind to bring your notebook to class?
Would you mind bringing your notebook to class?
Would you mind bring your notebook to class?
Would you mind brought your notebook to class?
questions.topic: Rewriting a command with 'Would you mind'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: After 'Would you mind' the verb must take -ing, so 'bringing' is correct.

questions.q: Change this order into a correct and polite sentence: *Stay after the lesson.*
options: I'm afraid you'll have to staying after the lesson.
I'm afraid you will to stay after the lesson.
I'm afraid you'll have stay after the lesson.
I'm afraid you'll have to stay after the lesson.
questions.topic: Softening an order with 'I'm afraid you'll have to'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'I'm afraid you'll have to + infinitive' makes a must-do request polite and grammatically correct.

questions.q: Which reply agrees politely with: *Can you carry these books for me?*
options: Of course.
Not at all.
You're welcome.
I'm sorry, I can't.
questions.topic: reply words for 'Can you ...?' requests
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: The lesson gives 'Certainly. / Of course. / Sure. / No problem.' as the agreement to 'Can you ...?'

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *You'll have ____ a visa before you travel abroad.*
options: to get
get
getting
got
questions.topic: the form after 'will have to'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: 'You'll have to' is followed by the base form of the verb, as in the lesson's 'you'll have to wait for an hour'.

questions.q: A: *Would you like to come to the science club on Sunday?* B cannot come. Which reply refuses politely?
options: I'm sorry, I can't.
Not at all.
Of course.
No problem.
questions.topic: polite refusal in a new dialogue
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: The lesson gives 'I'm sorry, I can't.' as one of the polite refusals, unlike the agreement words in the other options.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this request: *Could you to send this email?*
options: Could you send this email?
Could you sending this email?
Could you to sending this email?
Could you sends this email?
questions.topic: the base form after 'Could you'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: The lesson corrects 'Could you to help me?' to 'Could you help me?', so 'to' is not used after 'Could you'.

questions.q: A: *I'm afraid I can't lend you my bike tonight.* What does 'I'm afraid' do in this sentence?

questions.topic: the softening use of 'I'm afraid' in refusals
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)

questions.q: Re-order these words to make a polite request: *please / me / can / you / help / ?*

questions.topic: turning an order into a 'Would you ... please?' request
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)
questions.why: After 'Would you' we use the base form of the verb and add 'please' to make the order polite.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *You will have come at eight o'clock.*
options: You'll have to come at eight o'clock.

You'll have come at eight o'clock.
You would have to came at eight o'clock.
questions.topic: correcting 'will have come' to 'have to come'
questions.lesson: Being polite | التحدث بأدب (الطلبات المهذبة)

questions.q: What is a present participle?
options: A verb form made by adding -ing to a verb, as in playing, writing, drawing
A verb form made by adding -ed to a verb, as in played, walked, opened
A joining word that connects two sentences, as in and, but, so
A naming word made from a verb, as in driver, teacher, worker
questions.topic: Definition of the present participle (verb + ing)
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The lesson defines the present participle as a verb + ing, as in picking, smiling, running.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what do we use the present participle for?
options: To join two events that happened at the same time or nearly the same time into one sentence
To show that one event happened a long time before another event
To change a statement into a question about the past
To give an order to somebody in a polite way
questions.topic: Use of the present participle: joining two events at the same time
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The lesson says we use it to join two events that happened at the same time or nearly the same time in one sentence.

questions.q: What must be true about the two sentences before we can join them with a present participle?
options: The subject must be the same person in both sentences.
The two sentences must have exactly the same main verb.
The two events must be separated by a long period of time.
The second sentence must be shorter than the first sentence.
questions.topic: Condition for joining: the same subject in both sentences
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The lesson gives one condition: the subject in the two sentences must be the same person.

questions.q: When we join two sentences and the verb of the second sentence is past continuous (was/were + -ing), what do we delete from the second sentence?
options: The subject and was/were; we keep the verb with -ing.
The subject and the -ing form; we keep was/were.
Only the object; we keep the subject and was/were.
Nothing; we only put a comma between the two sentences.
questions.topic: Deleting the subject and was/were in the second sentence
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: Step 5 of the lesson: with was/were we drop the subject and the auxiliary and keep the -ing form, as in 'My father came in, smiling.'

questions.q: Combine the two sentences into one sentence using a present participle: *The girl walked home. She was singing.*
options: The girl walked home, singing.
The girl walked home, sang.
The girl walked home, she was singing.
The girl walked home, was singing.
questions.topic: Joining two sentences with a present participle
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: We delete 'She was' from the second sentence and keep the -ing form: The girl walked home, singing.

questions.q: Why can we NOT join these two sentences with a present participle? *She finished her homework. Her brother went to bed.*
options: Because the two sentences have different subjects.
Because the two verbs are in different tenses.
Because the second sentence has no object.
Because the two events did not happen at the same time.
questions.topic: Why two different subjects cannot be joined
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The subjects are 'She' and 'Her brother' — two different people, so the lesson's condition fails.

questions.q: What is the difference between sentence A and sentence B? A: *The man ran to the bus. He was carrying a bag.* B: *The man ran to the bus, carrying a bag.*
options: B joins the two events of A into one sentence with a present participle.
B changes the subject of the second event into an object.
B says the two events happened at different times, but A does not.
B is in the present tense, but A is in the past tense.
questions.topic: Comparing two separate sentences with one joined sentence
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: B does what the lesson describes: one comma, no subject for the second verb, just verb + ing.

questions.q: Complete the sentence correctly: *The boys sat under the tree, ____ .*
options: eating their lunch
they were eating their lunch
was eating their lunch
ate their lunch
questions.topic: Keeping the -ing form after deleting they and were
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: We delete 'they were' and keep the -ing form, so the joined sentence ends with 'eating their lunch'.

questions.q: Rewrite the two sentences as ONE sentence, beginning with the -ing part: *He was looking out of the window. He saw a strange light.*
options: Looking out of the window, he saw a strange light.
Looked out of the window, he saw a strange light.
He looking out of the window, saw a strange light.
Looking out of the window, he sees a strange light.
questions.topic: Rewriting the joined sentence with the -ing part first
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: Step 1: delete 'He was' and keep looking, then move the -ing part to the front of the sentence.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *She sat by the fire, she was reading a story.*
options: She sat by the fire, reading a story.
She sat by the fire, she read a story.
She sat by the fire, was reading a story.
She sat by the fire, read a story.
questions.topic: Correcting a wrongly joined sentence
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: Two clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; we drop 'she was' and keep the -ing form: reading.

questions.q: Choose the correct way to join the two sentences: *The teacher walked into the class. She was holding some books.*
options: The teacher walked into the class, holding some books.
The teacher walked into the class, she holding some books.
The teacher walked into the class, she was holding some books.
The teacher walked into the class and holding some books.
questions.topic: Joining two sentences after the main clause
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The repeated subject 'she' is dropped and 'was holding' becomes the participle 'holding' after the comma.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct form of the verb: *They sat in the garden, ____ about their holiday.* (talk)
options: talking
talked
talk
to talk
questions.topic: The -ing form of the verb after the comma
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: After the comma we use the present participle, so the verb 'talk' takes -ing and becomes 'talking'.

questions.q: In the sentence *My brother lay on the sofa, watching television*, which word is the present participle?
options: watching
lay
sofa
television
questions.topic: Identifying the present participle
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The present participle is the -ing form 'watching', which tells us what my brother was doing.

questions.q: Why is this sentence wrong? *Salem went to the market, his sister staying at home.*
options: Because the two parts do not have the same subject.
Because the participle should be in the past tense.
Because there is no comma before the participle.
Because 'staying' cannot come after a noun.
questions.topic: Different subjects cannot be joined
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: A participle joins two sentences only when both have the same subject, and here the subjects are Salem and his sister.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *'Thank you very much,' she said, ____ the present.* (accept)
options: accepting
accepted
accept
to accept
questions.topic: Participle clause after a reporting clause
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: After a reporting clause such as 'she said', the second action is joined with the present participle 'accepting'.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *The players ran onto the field, they shouting happily.*
options: The players ran onto the field, shouting happily.
The players ran onto the field, they shouting happily.
The players ran onto the field, shouted happily.
The players ran onto the field and shouting happily.
questions.topic: Repeating the subject before the -ing form
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The subject 'they' must be dropped before the -ing form, so we write 'shouting happily'.

questions.q: Compare: *Turning off the lights, she left the room.* / *She left the room, turning off the lights.* What do the two sentences have in common?
options: The -ing clause describes the same person in both sentences.
The -ing clause is the main verb in both sentences.
The -ing clause has its own subject in both sentences.
The -ing clause comes first in both sentences.
questions.topic: Same subject in both positions of the participle clause
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: Whether the participle comes first or last, it describes 'she', because both parts share the same subject.

questions.q: Rewrite the two sentences as ONE sentence, beginning with the present participle: *She heard the bad news. She began to cry.*
options: Hearing the bad news, she began to cry.
Heard the bad news, she began to cry.
She heard the bad news, beginning to cry.
Hearing the bad news and she began to cry.
questions.topic: Rewriting two sentences with a fronted participle clause
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: We start with the participle 'Hearing', drop the subject 'she' from the first sentence, and put a comma after the participle clause.

questions.q: Which sentence is INCORRECT because the two parts have different subjects?
options: Walking home from school, the rain started suddenly.
Waiting for the bus, the old man read a newspaper.
Looking for her keys, Mona opened her bag.
Standing at the gate, the children waved to their teacher.
questions.topic: Dangling participle with a wrong subject
questions.lesson: Joining ideas with the present participle | ربط فكرتين باسم الفاعل (الفعل + ing)
questions.why: The rain was not walking home, and a participle clause must share the subject of the main clause.

Language review 4 › Expressing obligatio.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل

questions.q: Complete the rule: We use must and have to + ____ to express obligation and necessity in the present and the future.
options: the infinitive of the main verb
the past participle of the main verb
the -ing form of the main verb
the main verb in the past simple form
questions.topic: must / have to + infinitive
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: The lesson states that have to and must are followed by the infinitive of a main verb to express obligation and necessity.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *Last week my brother ____ take our father to the hospital.*
options: had to
must
must to
has to
questions.topic: No 'must' in the past — had to
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: We cannot use must in the past, so the past form of obligation is had to + the infinitive.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *My sister ____ wear glasses when she reads.*
options: has to
have to
musts
having to
questions.topic: has to with he / she / it
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: With he, she or it we use has to + the infinitive, while I, you, we and they take have to.

questions.q: Complete the sentence about the future: *Next year my brother ____ travel to Cairo for his studies.*
options: will have to
will must
will has to
will have
questions.topic: will have to for future obligation
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: For a future obligation we use will have to + the infinitive; 'will must' is not correct English.

questions.q: Which sentence expresses an obligation that comes from outside the speaker, for example from another person or from circumstances?
options: Sami has to work on Friday because his manager asked him to.
Amina must study harder this term because she herself wants better marks.
I must tidy my room tonight because I have just decided to do it.
You must drink more water because I am worried about your health.
questions.topic: have to = obligation from outside
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: The lesson says have to usually shows an obligation coming from outside circumstances or from another person, as in the manager's request.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *The rules say you ____ be at the airport two hours before the flight.*
options: must or have to
must only, not have to
have to only, not must
must or has to
questions.topic: must and have to with the same meaning
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: In many sentences we can use either must or have to with almost the same meaning.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *She musts call her mother every evening.*
options: She must call her mother every evening.
She must to call her mother every evening.
She has must call her mother every evening.
She musts to call her mother every evening.
questions.topic: must never takes -s or -to
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: Must does not change with the pronoun and is followed directly by the infinitive without to.

questions.q: Why is 'must' correct in this sentence, although it talks about tomorrow? *You must bring your dictionary tomorrow.*
options: Because must expresses obligation in the present and the future.
Because must is the past form of have to.
Because must is always followed by the word 'to'.
Because must means that we are not obliged to do something.
questions.topic: must for the future as well as the present
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: The lesson says must and have to express obligation and necessity in the present and the future; only the past is impossible with must.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence in the past: *Mona has to look after her younger sister every evening.*
options: Mona had to look after her younger sister every evening.
Mona must looked after her younger sister every evening.
Mona had to looked after her younger sister every evening.
Mona must had to look after her younger sister every evening.
questions.topic: changing has to into had to
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: Must has no past form, so has to becomes had to, and the verb after it stays in the infinitive: had to look after.

questions.q: Make a question for the underlined words: *She had to leave the party early __because she felt tired__.*
options: Why did she have to leave the party early?
Why she had to leave the party early?
Why did she had to leave the party early?
Why did she has to leave the party early?
questions.topic: making a question with had to
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: After the auxiliary did we use the base form have to, and the question word comes first: Why did she have to leave ...?

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *You ____ finish your homework before you go out to play.*
options: must
must to
musts
to must
questions.topic: must + bare infinitive (no 'to')
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: After 'must' we use the infinitive without 'to' and without '-s', so 'must finish' is the correct form.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *Yesterday was a holiday, so I ____ wake up early.*
options: didn't have to
don't have to
didn't had to
hadn't to
questions.topic: didn't have to for no necessity in the past
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: The negative of 'had to' in the past is 'didn't have to', meaning it was not necessary.

questions.q: Complete the question: *____ your sister have to work at the weekend?*
options: Does
Do
Is
Has
questions.topic: Do/Does ... have to in questions
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: In present questions we use do/does + subject + have to, and 'your sister' takes 'Does'.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: He had to sell his car last year because he needed the money.
He must sell his car last year because he needed the money.
He musted sell his car last year because he needed the money.
He has to sell his car last year because he needed the money.
questions.topic: choosing had to for a past time reference
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: The past time 'last year' needs 'had to'; 'musted' is not a word, and 'must' and 'has to' cannot be used with a finished past time.

questions.q: Why is this sentence wrong? *I musted finish my report last night.*
options: Because 'must' has no past form, so we use 'had to' instead.
Because 'must' takes 'will' to make the past.
Because 'finish' should become 'finished' after 'musted'.
Because 'last night' needs the present perfect tense.
questions.topic: why 'musted' is not correct
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: 'Must' is a modal with no past form, so we cannot add '-ed'; the past of obligation is 'had to'.

questions.q: Rewrite this sentence about the past: *We have to wear a helmet at the building site.*
options: We had to wear a helmet at the building site.
We had to wore a helmet at the building site.
We musted wear a helmet at the building site.
We have had to wear a helmet at the building site.
questions.topic: changing a present obligation into the past
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: Change 'have to' into 'had to' and keep the verb after it in the infinitive: 'had to wear'.

questions.q: Rewrite this sentence in the future: *She has to look after her little brother.*
options: She will have to look after her little brother.
She will has to look after her little brother.
She will must look after her little brother.
She will have to looks after her little brother.
questions.topic: changing a present obligation into the future
questions.lesson: Expressing obligation and necessity - must و have to في الحاضر والماضي والمستقبل
questions.why: In the future 'has to' becomes 'will have to' and the verb after it stays in the infinitive without '-s'.
